scope: US data-center electricity demand forecasts through 2030-2031 and conversion factors to translate that load into US natural gas demand

forecasts.source: LBNL / DOE - United States Data Center Energy Usage Report: 2025 Update
forecasts.published: 2026-06 (IT shipment data through Q3 2025, assumptions as of Dec 2025)
forecasts.metric_basis: annual electricity consumption (TWh); GW is grid interconnection capacity assuming ~50% average utilization
forecasts.notes: Reference Case 649 TWh in 2030; sensitivity scenarios: Consolidated Deployment 578 TWh, High ASIC 664 TWh, Low Accelerator Lifetime 590 TWh, High Inference Energy 782 TWh; Compounded Uncertainty range 521-843 TWh. Data centers responsible for ~33% of all US load growth 2024-2030 under NERC LTRA forecast. Predecessor 2024 report (Dec 2024): 176 TWh in 2023 (4.4%); 2028 range 325-580 TWh (6.7-12.0% of US electricity, 74-132 GW at 50% utilization).

forecasts.source: EPRI - Powering Intelligence 2026 (Updated U.S. Data Center Scenarios)
forecasts.metric_basis: annual consumption (TWh) built up from state-level project pipeline; GW is IT capacity
forecasts.notes: 60% above EPRI's 2024 forecast (which saw 4.6-9.1% of US electricity by 2030) due to surge in announced/under-construction projects. Virginia data-center share could reach 41-59% of state electricity by 2030.

forecasts.metric_basis: power demand (GW) and share of US peak summer power demand
forecasts.notes: US data-center power demand projected to more than double from 31 GW (2025) to 66 GW (2027). Earlier GS work projected data-center power demand up ~175% by 2030 vs 2023 levels (roughly 84 GW-class outcome). No explicit 2030 GW point in the May 2026 public article.

forecasts.metric_basis: data-center power demand (GW) and share of US electricity consumption
forecasts.notes: July 2026 update raised 2035 US demand to 194 GW, 83% above the December 2025 forecast of 106 GW, reflecting ~150 new tracked projects (nearly a quarter over 500 MW each). Implies roughly 90-110 GW-class demand by 2030 on the new trajectory (BNEF does not publish the exact 2030 GW point publicly).
US data-center demand grows from ~25 GW (2024) to more than 80 GW by 2030; 147 TWh (2023) to ~606 TWh (2030), 11.7% of total US power demand.

forecasts.source: Deloitte - Can US infrastructure keep up with the AI economy?
forecasts.notes: Total US data-center demand 33 GW (2024) to as much as 176 GW (2035); AI portion grows ~30x from 4 GW to 123 GW (70% of total by 2035). Interpolated 2030 is roughly 90-100 GW on their published curve.

forecasts.source: Grid Strategies - National Load Growth Report 2025 (Strategic Industries series)
forecasts.metric_basis: utility/RTO peak load growth forecasts (GW) aggregated nationally
forecasts.notes: Aggregate utility forecasts show +166 GW US peak load by 2030, ~55% (about 90 GW) tied to data centers; Grid Strategies believes utility figures are somewhat overstated and market-based data-center growth by 2030 is likelier ~65 GW.

forecasts.metric_basis: annual consumption (TWh); US figures broken out from global
forecasts.notes: US data centers consumed ~183 TWh in 2024 (>4% of US electricity). IEA's US 2030 projection (~430 TWh) is the low outlier among major forecasts; LBNL's 2025 Update explicitly flags it as substantially below their 649 TWh Reference Case.

forecasts.published: 2025-2026 (US Grid Constraints and Onsite Gas Deep Dive posts)
forecasts.notes: Cumulative confirmed behind-the-meter critical IT capacity reaches ~26 GW by end-2030 (likely higher with unannounced projects); BTM becomes the primary power source for ~half of new AI data-center capacity additions by 2028, up from under 7% of 2025 additions.

forecasts.source: EIA - Annual Energy Outlook 2026 / STEO commentary
forecasts.metric_basis: long-run server consumption (BkWh) and total US electricity demand
forecasts.notes: EIA frames data centers as the dominant driver of long-term US electricity growth but publishes server-only consumption, not an all-in data-center 2030 GW point. STEO has US power consumption at record highs in 2025 and 2026, led by commercial-sector (data-center) sales; commercial sales overtake residential in 2027 for the first time on record.

actuals.us_data_center_consumption_2025_note: 2025 TWh is an interpolation on the LBNL 2025-Update Reference Case (192 TWh in 2024 to 464 TWh in 2028); LBNL treats 2024 as the last fully historical year. EPRI puts 2024 at 177-192 TWh.
actuals.current_share_of_us_electricity_pct: about 4.7-5.5% of US consumption in 2025, on track for 6%+ in 2026

conversion_factors.method: MMcf/d per GW running 24/7 = heat_rate_mmbtu_per_mwh x 24,000 MWh/day / 1,037 Btu per cf (EIA average heat content of consumed natural gas, i.e. 1,037 MMBtu per MMcf)
conversion_factors.example_math: 1 GW at 6.4 MMBtu/MWh -> 6.4 x 24,000 = 153,600 MMBtu/day / 1,037 = ~148 MMcf/d

technologies.technology: H-class combined-cycle gas turbine (new build, e.g. GE Vernova 7HA)
technologies.note: Best-in-class new CCGT, ~53-56% HHV efficiency. Homer City's disclosed ~665,000 MMBtu/day for ~4.4 GW works out to 6.3 MMBtu/MWh and ~146 MMcf/d per GW, corroborating this band.

technologies.technology: Aeroderivative / simple-cycle peaker (LM2500/LM6000-class, frame simple cycle)
technologies.note: Fast-deploy bridging power widely used at BTM data-center sites (xAI, Stargate Abilene). Rarely run at 24/7 baseload long-term, but many data-center bridge units do run at high capacity factors.
~38-42% efficiency; favored for fast delivery and load-following at off-grid campuses.

Bloom claims ~54% point-of-use electrical efficiency (vs 35-40% simple-cycle), i.e. 3.412/0.54 = ~6.3 MMBtu/MWh -> ~146 MMcf/d per GW, matching the widely cited ~150 MMcf/d per GW figure. Oracle MSA up to 2.8 GW (Apr 2026), AEP up to 1 GW, Brookfield partnership announced 2026.

recommended_single_factor.rationale: New efficient generation (H-class CCGT or Bloom SOFC, heat rate ~6.3 MMBtu/MWh) at 100% capacity factor gives ~145-148 MMcf/d per GW; independently corroborated by Homer City's disclosed 665,000 MMBtu/day for 4.4 GW (~146 MMcf/d per GW). Use 0.15 Bcf/d per GW as base; a fleet-average mix with peakers/recips runs 0.17-0.20 Bcf/d per GW.

gas_share_estimates.estimate: Natural gas is already the largest source of electricity for US data centers at >40% share (2024). To 2030, renewables meet nearly half of incremental global data-center demand; gas-fired generation expands ~175 TWh globally, concentrated in the US, where gas remains the largest single supply source through 2030.

Behind-the-meter generation (predominantly gas turbines, recips, and fuel cells) supplies ~50% of new AI data-center capacity additions by 2028, up from <7% of 2025 additions; ~26 GW of confirmed BTM critical IT capacity by end-2030.
~81 GW of new gas-fired power capacity tied to data-center demand by 2030 across ~290 tracked projects, implying 4.2-6.1 Bcf/d of incremental US gas demand.
Base case ~+3 Bcf/d of US gas demand from data centers by 2030, upside approaching 6 Bcf/d depending on infrastructure buildout pace.
Incremental gas demand from data centers of 3-6 Bcf/d by 2030; dedicated/co-located gas generation seen as the best-fit supply given grid constraints.

Behind-the-meter projects ~40% of announced off-grid installed capacity; implies ~1.3 Bcf/d of incremental gas demand by 2030 (about half in ERCOT and PJM) - the conservative end of published estimates.

gas_share_estimates.consensus_note: Published incremental US gas demand from data centers by 2030 clusters at 3-6 Bcf/d (East Daley 4.2-6.1; S&P base 3, upside 6; Kinder Morgan 3-6; Enverus 1.3 as low outlier). At 0.15 Bcf/d per GW, that range implies roughly 20-40 GW of gas-served data-center load.

btm_projects.gw_note: Oracle master services agreement up to 2.8 GW (Apr 2026) + AEP up to 1 GW

btm_projects.status: framework agreements; deployments ramping; Bloom targeting 2 GW/yr manufacturing capacity; $25B Brookfield commitment Jul 2026

notes: Definitional caution: forecasts mix three metrics - annual consumption (TWh), average power demand (GW), IT/nameplate capacity (GW), and requested grid interconnection capacity (GW). LBNL assumes ~50% average utilization of interconnection capacity, so 649 TWh (74 GW average load) maps to ~148 GW of interconnection requests in 2030.

2030 US forecast convergence: consumption estimates cluster at 380-850 TWh (IEA ~430 low outlier; EPRI 380-790; LBNL 521-843, reference 649; McKinsey ~606). Capacity-basis estimates for 2030 span ~65 GW (Grid Strategies market view) to ~148 GW (LBNL interconnection), with utility filings at ~90 GW of data-center peak growth.
Texas alone had an estimated ~38 GW of behind-the-meter data-center generation in development as of early 2026 (Texas Tribune/DCD reporting).
Announced BTM pipelines exceed what published gas-demand forecasts assume gets built; East Daley's 81 GW of DC-linked gas capacity by 2030 is a tracker of projects, not a realization forecast.

Gas math sanity check: Homer City contracts ~665,000 MMBtu/day for ~4.4 GW = 6.3 MMBtu/MWh heat rate = ~146 MMcf/d per GW, essentially identical to Bloom SOFC at claimed 54% efficiency. This makes ~0.15 Bcf/d per 24/7 GW the most defensible single conversion for new efficient capacity.

All Bcf/d incremental-demand estimates (3-6 Bcf/d by 2030) are small against ~107 Bcf/d total US gas demand but large against power-sector gas burn growth; timing risk is concentrated in 2027-2029 turbine delivery slots.
